## [The unreliable witness](https://seths.blog/2026/10/the-unreliable-witness/)

It might be us.

Even when there are photos, videos or tape recordings, people find that they can’t agree on what happened.

Our vivid recollections can be vivid, but they might not be accurate.

What would happen if, for a moment, we imagined that our version of what happened might not be the only one?

title: Leap Seconds Have Helped Keep Clocks Synchronized with Earth’s Rotation, But Their Time May Be Over
content:
You’re probably used to the month of February having an extra day every four years, during the [leap year](https://theconversation.com/why-does-a-leap-year-have-366-days-218330). Timekeepers added that extra leap day because Earth completes one orbit around the Sun in about 365 and one-quarter days. If we didn’t add leap days, the equinoxes and solstices that mark the beginning of seasons would occur later, slowly shifting the days on which each season began.

For millennia, a day has been defined as one full rotation of the Earth. But the Earth’s rotation [isn’t completely uniform](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/news/feature-articles/when-day-day), and in order to be more precise, modern timekeeping systems have stopped using the Earth’s rotation as their basis.

This switch created a discrepancy between how a single second used to be defined, and how it is defined today.

Over the course of several years, modern time systems can become a few seconds out of sync with the Earth’s movement. To solve this issue, timekeepers use what’s called a leap second. Just as leap years keep our calendars in alignment with Earth’s orbit around the Sun, leap seconds have kept our timekeeping aligned with Earth’s daily rotation.

But in October 2026, an international organization governing timekeeping [may change its strategy](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/international-timekeepers-to-vote-on-changing-the-leap-second-to-a-leap-hour/) for adding leap seconds.

As a [space scientist](https://dornsife.usc.edu/profile/vahe-peroomian/), I know how measuring time is fundamental to physics research. The precision of physicists’ measurements has gotten better as the way we measure time has changed.

**History of Seconds**

The systems humans use to measure time have evolved over the past few centuries.

The origin of the 24-hour day can be traced to the second millennium B.C.E., when [ancient Egyptians](https://www.britannica.com/topic/24-hour-clock) divided day and night into 12 parts each. Because the length of day and night varies during the year, the length of each hour of daylight and each hour of night did as well.

The [Greek astronomer Hipparchus](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hipparchus-Greek-astronomer), who lived in the second century B.C.E., later adopted a system using 24 equal hours for astronomical calculations.

The division of an hour into 60 minutes of 60 seconds each also has its roots in astronomy. Division by 60, or [a base-60 system](https://theconversation.com/what-was-the-first-thing-scientists-discovered-a-historian-makes-the-case-for-babylonian-astronomy-244463), traces back to the Sumerian and Babylonian [civilizations of Mesopotamia](https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20260320-the-ancient-reason-there-are-60-minutes-in-an-hour-and-60-seconds-in-a-minute). The number 60 is particularly convenient because it can be divided up evenly into smaller parts.

The Greek astronomer [Claudius Ptolemy](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ptolemy) adopted the base-60 system while measuring the motions of planets around 150 C.E. He divided each angular degree into 60 parts, and each of these into 60 smaller parts. In Latin, these were later called _partes minutae primae_, or “first small parts,” and _partes minutae secundae:_ “second small parts.” This system eventually led to the words “minute” and “second.”

Centuries later, as mechanical clocks became increasingly precise, these astronomical subdivisions were adopted for timekeeping as well. Based on the systems devised by Ptolemy and his successors, a mean solar day was divided into 24 hours, times 60 minutes per hour, times 60 seconds per minute: 86,400 seconds.

However, actually measuring time down to the second only became possible after Christiaan Huygens [invented the pendulum clock in 1657](https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2017/06/huygens-patents-first-pendulum-clock). In a pendulum clock, a suspended weight swings back and forth at a steady rate. As long as you take the differences in the Earth’s gravitational pull into account, all pendulums of the same length complete a swing in the same length of time. This metric provided a standardized way to measure time.

**The Leap Day and Leap Second**

In the spirit of the pendulum clock, scientists spent three more centuries developing systems that would measure time precisely and in a standardized way so that all clocks around the world could tell the same time. During this process, the definition of a second changed several times. They finally found a solution in the cesium atom.

In 1967, the [General Conference on Weights and Measures](https://www.bipm.org/en/committees/cg/cgpm) – an intergovernmental organization that sets measurement standards and has over 100 member nations today – adopted a new definition based on the [cesium-133 atom](https://www.nist.gov/atomic-clocks/how-atomic-clocks-work/beams-atoms-first-atomic-clocks).

Cesium-133 atoms behave like [extraordinarily precise clocks](https://theconversation.com/using-atomic-nuclei-could-allow-scientists-to-read-time-more-precisely-than-ever-what-this-research-could-mean-for-future-clocks-272017). When the atom switches between two particular energy states, it produces radiation that oscillates, just like a pendulum, at a remarkably steady rate. Scientists defined 1 second as exactly 9,192,631,770 of these oscillations.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ExYZyvK0b_M)

[Coordinated Universal Time](https://www.nist.gov/pml/time-and-frequency-division/time-realization/utcnist-time-scale), UTC, is [based on atomic clocks](https://www.nist.gov/pml/time-and-frequency-division/how-utcnist-related-coordinated-universal-time-utc-international) that use cesium-133. As a result, [UT1](https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/UT), the time scale based on Earth’s rotation, can drift relative to UTC.

This divergence reflects both short-term irregularities in how fast Earth rotates, and a very gradual, long-term slowdown of Earth’s rotation, [caused primarily by](https://theconversation.com/the-moon-is-getting-slightly-farther-away-from-the-earth-each-year-a-physicist-explains-why-262106) the [Moon’s gravitational pull](https://www.britannica.com/science/tidal-friction) on Earth’s oceans.

The difference between the 86,400 atomic seconds metric and a day measured by Earth’s rotation is less than [4 milliseconds](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/earth-rotation.html). This discrepancy may seem small, but it can accumulate to a significant fraction of a second over the course of a year.

Since 1972, timekeepers have added 27 positive leap seconds to UTC, at very irregular intervals. Their aim has been to keep the discrepancy between UTC and UT1 to less than 0.9 seconds. They added the [last leap second at the end of 2016](https://www.nist.gov/pml/time-and-frequency-division/time-realization/leap-seconds).

**The End of the Leap Second**

Adding a second to clocks every so often can disrupt high-precision computer systems. Many computer operating systems assume that a day is 86,400 seconds long and that time advances in a predictable, monotonically increasing sequence. Adding a leap second violates both of those assumptions. On days when a leap second is added, clocks jump by one second on the designated day. That day is then 86,401 seconds long.

In 2012, for example, [Reddit experienced an outage](https://www.wired.com/2012/07/leap-second-glitch-explained/) after a leap second was added on June 30 of that year. Other systems, including the Linux kernel and some Java-based applications, [were also affected](https://observer.com/2012/07/june-30-leap-second-bug-briefly-knocks-out-reddit-foursquare/).

Because of incidents like these, many high-profile technology companies, including Google and Meta, use “[smearing](https://medium.com/@vishalkamath853/how-google-handles-leap-seconds-877da8252620),” where they spread the extra second in gradual increments over a long time period, rather than inserting it as a one-second step. This endeavor is not easy, and these companies are strongly advocating for [abolishing the leap second](https://engineering.fb.com/2022/07/25/production-engineering/its-time-to-leave-the-leap-second-in-the-past/).

In 2022, the General Conference on Weights and Measures decided the maximum difference between UTC and UT1 should be increased in, or before, 2035. They planned to agree upon a new maximum value at their 2026 meeting.

One factor accelerating their decision is that the Earth has experienced a period of unusually rapid rotation [since about 2015](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/earth-faster-rotation.html). During the 2020 calendar year, timekeepers recorded 28 days where the Earth completed its full rotation before the clock hit 86,400 atomic seconds. The shortest day measured in the modern atomic-clock era occurred on June 29, 2022, when the Earth completed its rotation [1.59 milliseconds](https://www.timeanddate.com/news/astronomy/shortest-day-2022) faster than 86,400 atomic seconds.

If Earth keeps up this faster rotation, timekeepers might eventually need to introduce the first-ever negative leap second. There’s no large-scale precedent for how computer systems would handle one, which is why the issue has taken on new urgency.

The General Conference on Weights and Measures will meet Oct. 13-15, 2026. It is considering a draft resolution that would make UTC a continuous time scale, without the abrupt addition of leap seconds, beginning on May 20, 2027.

The resolution would allow the difference between UTC and UT1 to grow as large as 3,600 seconds, or one hour. This is akin to replacing the leap second with a “leap hour.” The resolution does not specify a schedule for inserting discrete one-hour corrections. A leap hour would not be necessary for centuries.

**Will I Notice the Change?**

The clocks on your smartphones, laptops and other electronic devices seldom, if ever, display seconds. Because of this, the addition of leap seconds has typically gone unnoticed by all but [the metrologists responsible](https://careercenter.ies.org/career/metrologist) for various timekeeping systems.

As UTC and UT1 are allowed to diverge, astronomers, Earth scientists and other users of Earth-orientation data will need to account for the growing offset when relating their observations and measurements to civil time.

Navigating using the positions of the Sun, the Moon, and the stars requires knowing the precise time when observations are made. Celestial navigators who do this will need to account for the growing difference between UTC and UT1 when determining their precise position on Earth.

When you use a compass for navigation, you must take into account the difference between the location of Earth’s magnetic and geographic poles. You can do so by factoring in the [magnetic declination](https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-declination) of your location, or the angle between the direction the compass is pointing in and true north. Software on smartphones can do this automatically.

A similar approach already exists for converting between UTC, UT1 and other time scales in use today. If the draft resolution is adopted in October, keeping track of the differences between these time scales, especially the drift between UTC and UT1, would become a more important part of high-precision timekeeping.

By mid-October, the leap second may be a thing of the past. Given the importance that people attach to the regular change of seasons, though, the leap year is not going anywhere. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Key to Multilingualism Lies in the Ears, Not the Mouth
content:
Steve Martin’s [favorite](https://people.com/steve-martin-pink-panther-favorite-comic-scene-ever-done-exclusive-11902595) comic moment of his entire career is the “hamburger” scene from _The Pink Panther_ (2006), he once told _People_ magazine. Martin plays Inspector Clouseau, who has an aggressively exaggerated French accent. In the scene, he is trying to [learn](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z6oeAdemFZw) how to say, “I would like to buy a hamburger,” with a dialect coach. “Dam-buergaaaaa,” he purrs at his coach, along with increasingly ridiculous permutations of all of the other words in the sentence.

The scene is funny because it’s true for so many of us: Learning a new language as an adult can be hard. The unfamiliar sounds may get tangled up in the mouth like marbles, and the results can sound like gibberish. But for other people, new foreign words seem to roll off the tongue and adopting different accents comes easily. Their secret may lie in how they listen, according to a new [study](https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/xge0001991) in the _Journal of Experimental Psychology_. People who are better at detecting small differences in the frequency of raw sound are better at picking up new foreign speech sounds, and thus might be quicker to learn new languages, the study found.

**“Read more:**[**Speaking More Languages May Help Slow Brain Aging**](https://nautil.us/speaking-more-languages-may-help-slow-brain-aging-1282456)**”**

“Most people approach foreign language learning by memorizing vocabulary and listening to speech, but our study indicated that language learners might also benefit from training the auditory abilities that underpin language learning itself,” said study author Kazuya Sait-van Poeteren of the UCL Institute of Education in London, in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1147188). “Foreign language education should move beyond an approach based on ‘more practice’ and towards one that develops learners’ ear for language learning in line with their auditory characteristics.”

Sait-van Poeteren and colleagues from the United Kingdom, Japan, and Switzerland studied Japanese students learning the English vowels in a series of word pairs, such as “mad” versus “mud.” In an initial experiment, they delivered a test of auditory perception to 140 people online. These participants were tasked with figuring out which of three artificial tones was not like the others, based on small shifts in frequency. They also listened to spoken English and were asked to identify the words they heard. In a second experiment, 67 people underwent a brain scan while they judged whether pairs of English words and pairs of non-speech tones were the same or different.

What the team found: The more minute differences in tones people could discern, the better they were at telling the words in the pairs apart. While time spent studying abroad or getting training in pronunciation also made a significant difference, auditory perception mattered even when accounting for these differences in experience. It was a medium-sized effect and showed up in both experiments.

Having a good ear for small shifts in sound frequency was also linked to differences in how the brain processed the words from a new language. The learners who scored less well on hearing differences in non-speech sounds seemed to rely more on parts of the brain’s sensorimotor cortex, which is responsible for movement planning and feedback when hearing the English vowels. But this pattern wasn’t detected for the non-speech tones.

Sait-van Poeteren and his colleagues wrote that adults who are less skilled at hearing differences in sound may try to map unfamiliar words onto sounds in their own native language, partly by silently simulating how they’d say it. This can keep them stuck. People with sharp hearing may be able to bypass this filter, though, tuning out their linguistic past, and treating new sound more like raw acoustics, though the study didn’t demonstrate that directly. Their hypothesis aligns with the results of earlier [studies](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13414-022-02463-w) that suggest that requiring learners to pronounce a new sound too early can [interfere](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13423-024-02561-w) with how well they learn to hear it.

The new study findings echo [previous](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0093934X19300033?via%3Dihub)[work](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0749596X20300826?via%3Dihub) by the same group that shows that strong auditory perception that is not tied to speech is predictive of better pronunciation when a person is learning a second language. But these earlier studies mostly showed a behavioral link. The current study is among the first to use brain imaging to try to tease out how weaker or stronger auditory precision relates to brain activity during second-language listening.

Musical training was not a major predictor of the participants’ skill at hearing differences between the words in the new language. What mattered was the measured ability to hear small acoustic differences.

Clouseau’s trouble with that hamburger seemed to lie in the mouth—with each new attempt he would contort his lips into a new shape to try to capture the word. But the new research suggests that when learning a new language, it’s best to start by fine tuning the ears. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Can GLP-1s Slow Aging?
content:
GLP-1 medications are wildly popular for shedding excess weight, but they seem to offer a wide-range of ancillary health benefits, too. Early studies show they improve kidney function, [bolster](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.126.079319) our cardiovascular systems, and even help [curb addiction](https://med.stanford.edu/news/insights/2025/04/ozempic-addiction-glp-1s-mounjaro-lembke.html). Could they also help slow the effects of aging?

The answer is a resounding yes, according to the drug companies that manufacture and sell them.

**Read more: “**[**Is This Metabolic Molecule from Pythons the Next Big Weight-Loss Drug?”**](https://nautil.us/is-this-metabolic-molecule-from-pythons-the-next-big-weight-loss-drug-1279047)

Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk (the makers of tirzepatide and semaglutide, respectively) announced last week that their drugs are also associated with a reduction in biological age. (The “biological age” is the age as measured by [molecular clocks](https://nautil.us/a-peek-inside-the-black-box-of-epigenetic-clocks-1283841), which typically track epigenetic changes in a series of genes, including those involved in metabolic pathways.)

Representatives from both companies unveiled data at the 13th annual Aging Research & Drug Discovery conference showing that people taking the drugs have molecular ages two to three years younger (compared to those who took only placebos). Measures from a molecular clock that tracks proteins related to the heart showed a four-year reduction.

Does that mean these drugs can really slow aging?

It’s hard to say. The data, which was gathered during clinical trials for the medications, has yet to be analyzed by a third-party and the findings haven’t undergone peer review. Additionally, the trials were conducted in those who were already overweight and diabetic, not healthy adults. Finally, GLP-1s are relatively new (as are molecular clocks), and any research showing significant longevity benefits will likely take some time.

Still, there’s reason to believe these drugs may offer hope for lengthening our lifespans. Again, GLP-1s have effects that extend beyond weight loss, acting on different organ systems. Unfortunately, they have side effects as well, and some of them—like [muscle loss](https://nautil.us/muscle-loss-is-a-big-warning-sign-of-dementia-1285125)—could cause additional problems.

It’s going to take some time—and some research conducted by people whose paychecks aren’t signed by drug companies—to find out for sure. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Mere Minutes With AI Causes a Sharp Drop in Persistence
content:
New York City schools took the drastic action of restricting artificial intelligence last month, banning around 600,000 students from pre-K through eighth grade from using the technology. “They learn best when they are wrestling with hard problems, when they’re getting it wrong, when they’re trying again and finally getting it right,” the chancellor of schools Kamar Samuels [said](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/01/nyregion/ai-ban-schools-nyc.html) of the move. “No app, chatbot, or algorithm can replicate that productive struggle for a child.”

Rather than replicate it, AI is promising to eliminate it entirely (at least for adults). Now a new [study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.04721) presented this week at the third annual Conference on Language Modeling is providing more evidence that AI could erode our critical cognitive faculties.

**Read more: “**[**A Recipe to Stop AI from Going Rogue**](https://nautil.us/a-recipe-for-stopping-ai-from-going-rogue-1285647)**”**

To investigate how AI might shape our long-term learning, AI researchers led by Brian Christian of University of California Berkeley designed a series of test-taking experiments. Adult participants were tasked with solving a series of equations involving fractions (e.g., 5/6 minus 1/3). One group was provided with a ChatGPT window to help, while the other had to slog through solo. After a series of questions, ChatGPT disappeared, leaving the former group to finish the test with nothing but their brains as well.

The researchers found that the members of the ChatGPT group solved the problems at a higher rate than the control group and skipped questions at a lower rate—at least until it was taken away. After the chatbot disappeared, the two groups swapped places, with the brain-only crowd solving at a higher rate and skipping questions at a lower rate.

The mean results of the first experiment showed a drop-off in the solve rate for the ChatGPT group and an increase in the rate at which they skipped questions. _Credit: Brian Christian et al_

To find out if the effect extends beyond mathematics, the team repeated the experiment with reading comprehension questions cribbed from SAT exams. The researchers uncovered the same dynamic—the persistence and accuracy of the group leaning on the AI tool dropped when it was gone.

It’s a striking finding. Over the course of tests that lasted mere minutes, those who relied on AI seemed more prone to giving up. “You almost couldn’t ask for a clearer story,” Christian said in a [statement](https://news.berkeley.edu/2026/10/09/using-ai-for-just-10-minutes-erodes-your-ability-to-persist-at-hard-things/). “We’ve built these systems to be helpful, but are they being helpful to us in a way that’s actually helping us? We showed, ironically, that they’re often helping us in ways that are kind of unhelpful.”

For students, the researchers say this could lead to a “boiling frog” problem. “If sustained AI use erodes the motivation and persistence that drive long-term learning, these effects will accumulate over years, and by the time they are visible, they will be difficult to reverse,” they wrote.

And this study only examines the effects of AI bots that can capably answer questions. What happens if there’s widespread adoption of AI agents like Meta’s Muse that promise to eliminate the productive struggle from the rest of our lives too?

In a frictionless world, some of us may be in danger of slipping away.![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: These New Snails Can Slam Shut Their Shells Like Doors
content:
Most of us who have been teenagers know the unique satisfaction of seeking refuge behind a shut door. So do these two new snail species in Montenegro that boast tiny openings on their shells that can be closed like doors.

After a hard day of slowly sliming around the neighborhood, it must be a relief to shut out the rest of the world and get some peace and quiet. These openings (or “operculum”) are common in freshwater and sea snails, but not in European land snails like the two found here—a clue to the ancestry of the species.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kuv8S5JK8sU)

By sealing up their shells, the snails are able to trap moisture in and keep predators out. Other snails use a temporary layer of mucus for the same thing.

Another feature that distinguishes these creatures from most land snails is the position of the eyes on the sides of their heads, rather than on stalks. Both species measure under 0.28 inches long and live in limestone rocks, with algae and lichens making up their daily diet.

**Read more: “**[**How Snails Cross Vast Oceans**](https://nautil.us/how-snails-cross-vast-oceans-288802)**”**

The new species, detailed [in a recent study](https://bdj.pensoft.net/article/196955/), are _Cochlostoma komarnica_ and _Cochlostoma dobrido_, names that reflect where they were found: the Komarnica Canyon and the Dobri Do Plateau, respectively.

Shells collected by researchers: C. komarnica on the left, C. dobrido on the right. _Credit: Enrico Zallot_

_C. komarnica_ tends to live a little lower down in terms of altitude than _C. dobrido_. In wet weather, they were observed foraging and exploring, while dry weather saw them take refuge in cracks and rocks and under moss—the snail equivalent of the patio umbrella.

Any new species discovery helps in the cataloging and protection of wildlife, but there’s a particularly urgent conservation angle to the _C. komarnica_ snail. The canyon it was found in is scheduled to be flooded as part of a hydropower dam and reservoir project. “This will destroy this wild river canyon and all the biodiversity in it, including many species still unknown to science,” study author Jovana Đokić explained in a [statement](https://blog.pensoft.net/2026/07/27/new-snail-species-bolster-case-for-protecting-montenegros-biodiversity/).

To help ensure the future of _C. komarnica_, the study team is calling for the canyon to be added to the existing UNESCO World Heritage site of Durmitor. After all, it’s going to take more than a shell door to protect these animals if the dam project goes ahead. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Let The People Set The Pace Of Frontier AI
content:
Credits

Hélène Landemore is the Damon Wells ‘58 professor of political science at Yale University and distinguished researcher at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI.

Audrey Tang is Taiwan’s cyber ambassador and founding minister of digital affairs, a Carnegie distinguished fellow at Columbia University School of International and Public Affairs, a senior fellow at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI, a senior research fellow at the Collective Intelligence Project and a 2025 Right Livelihood Laureate.

Those building the most powerful AI systems in the world are increasingly telling us that the race to build them may be moving too fast. But there is a problem: They cannot simply agree to slow down.

On Sept. 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for an easing of the pace at which AI models improve and committed his company to giving independent, third-party evaluators ongoing, employee-like access to its systems. Amodei further gestured toward “democratic coordination” on shared safety limits and “global coordination” on the international stage. Within hours, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed that “we need to pace the frontier” and made the same evaluator pledge. Elon Musk’s response was three words: “Dario is right.”

This apparent convergence among the leaders of the frontier AI labs is striking. It comes after months of mounting concern inside and outside the industry: AI models have begun to find ways around safeguards and test environments; researchers have left frontier labs amid disagreements over catastrophic and extinction-level risks; and more than 1,300 employees at leading AI companies have called on Washington to back an international slowdown.

But even if the CEOs agree, the race does not stop.

The reason is structural. The two governments with the greatest capacity to shape the frontier AI race — in Washington and Beijing — have powerful incentives not to be the first to slow down. Each has reason to fear that restraint on their part will simply hand a strategic advantage to the other.

What we are facing, in other words, is a double collective-action problem, one nested under the other. The two are linked: “If we slow down, China wins” is the main argument American labs and government officials use against binding regulation. The outer race is the inner one’s best excuse; end the global race, and the domestic one loses cover. The good news is that, contrary to frequent depictions, neither is a simple prisoner’s dilemma, in which each player’s best strategy is to defect no matter what others do, and also that the only solution is necessarily some sort of global regulatory leviathan.

Instead, both collective-action problems look more like what game theorists call a “stag hunt,” after a parable of Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s. A party of hunters sets out after a stag. It will take all of them to bring it down, and it will feed them all for days. Along the way, each hunter sees a hare and considers catching it. The hare is a thin meal but a sure one, though if even a single hunter breaks off to chase one, the stag escapes and the rest go home hungry. Nobody in the party prefers the hare. A hunter settles for it only after losing faith that the others will hold the line in the quest for the stag.

The stag, here, is a frontier paced long enough to make safe; the hare is the lead a single lab or a single country can take by racing on alone. A lab or a country that trusted its rivals would do better by pacing alongside them, since a shared slowdown is worth more than a temporary lead that might ruin everyone, the leader included.

> “The two governments with the greatest capacity to shape the frontier AI race have powerful incentives not to be the first to slow down.”

The way out of a stag hunt is not coercion but an assurance mechanism. If each player can believe that the others will keep their post and, even better, watch them keeping to their posts, the fear that pulls the party apart loses its grip. The frontier does not have to be placed under a single world power to be slowed down and controlled. But it needs assurance, and assurance requires two things: verification and a witness that is credible to all parties.

The first is already taking shape. The independent evaluators Anthropic and OpenAI pledged to permit would see inside frontier systems with employee-like access and could report whether a lab is keeping its pace. But evaluators engaged by the labs, judging against risk thresholds the labs themselves define, cannot reassure a rival, let alone a rival government. Evidence changes what the hunters believe about one another only when it flows to someone none of them controls, and who has set the standard it is measured against.

What is needed to nudge all players toward the cooperative equilibrium, therefore, is a body with enough moral authority to be an obvious coordination point and with the political legitimacy to set the terms of cooperation, coordinate the verification process and raise the reputational costs for any form of defection. What existing body has such moral authority and political legitimacy in the world today?

The obvious candidate is the United Nations, which is the closest thing we have to a standing witness for the world’s affairs. But the U.N. is not a neutral bystander here: It is structurally entangled with the very powers whose rivalry drives the race. The Security Council grants Washington and Beijing each a veto over the institution meant to referee them. More deeply, the U.N. is built out of nation-states and speaks in their voice and language. It is an assembly of sovereigns, not a body that can stand above sovereignty and weigh it against humanity’s interests.

If not the U.N., then who? One contender has a stronger claim than any institution, on this issue and many others: humanity itself, whose interests, and indeed survival, are crucially at stake in whether the race continues unabated or is tamed. Humanity alone stands above AI CEOs, the governments in Washington and Beijing, other competing nations, international boards of experts and even the U.N. in its credibility to say “Stop!” or “Slow down” or “We want AI to do this but not that.” That is because humanity’s stake is universal and undiluted by any single national or corporate interest.

AI CEOs recognize the claims of humanity openly. In March 2023 and in multiple interviews since then, Altman [laid out](https://podscript.ai/podcasts/lex-fridman-podcast/367-sam-altman-openai-ceo-on-gpt-4-chatgpt-and-the-future-of-ai/) a “dream scenario” that “every person on Earth would come together, have a really thoughtful, deliberative conversation about where we want to draw the boundary on this system, and we would have something like the U.S. Constitutional Convention, where we debate the issues and we look at things from different perspectives.” To the question “Why pace?” Amodei answered that “society must have a say in how this technology is used” and that pacing would buy time for “public deliberations.” He did not say which society he had in mind. It cannot be America alone, or even the West in general — a technology with global consequences calls for a global deliberation.

Of course, humanity has no voice of its own in the existing international order. But we could give it one through careful design.

Our proposal is a standing global citizens’ assembly of 1,000 people chosen by lot from around the world — call it the Global Citizens’ Assembly on AI. This assembly would be charged with helping to set the purposes and limits of powerful AI, and with receiving the evaluators’ findings on whether those limits are kept. What must AI never be allowed to do? What do we want it to do for us and for those who come after us? Who should govern it, and by which principles? These are questions to be answered by humanity as a whole, and short of that a representative sample of it.

> Humanity alone stands above AI CEOs, the governments in Washington and Beijing, other competing nations, international boards of experts and even the U.N. in its credibility to say ‘Stop!'”

The assembly would sit continuously rather than produce a single report. Members would serve fixed, part-time terms, with a third of the seats regularly redrawn by lot, so that the body keeps its memory without hardening into a class of its own. While they serve, members would deliberate over months, online and with local support, with financial compensation for their time and expenses, translation and interpretation, secure communication, and protection for those whose governments may dislike what they say. An independent civic secretariat would pool disclosed funding from participating governments and labs without letting funders influence recruitment or tamper with evidence.

Members could commission competing expertise, and anyone outside the assembly would have a published route to challenge its selection and its findings. Ideally, the assembly would also be connected to local and national processes whose input would feed into its deliberations. Earlier versions of these designs appeared in [Fortune](https://fortune.com/europe/2023/06/20/why-picking-citizens-at-random-best-way-to-govern-ai-revolution-tech-politics/) in 2023 and in [Noema](https://www.noemamag.com/how-to-give-everyday-people-a-say-in-ai-governance/) this August.

Why 1,000 global citizens? Is this not unwieldy? If basic demographic representativeness were the sole goal, a statistician might settle for a few hundred members. We ask for 1,000 for a different reason: symbolism and the salience that comes with size. A body the size of a large parliament is not a focus group, and cannot simply be ignored. A CEO can shrug off a critic, even a panel of experts. But any lab leader who refuses to answer a thousand people drawn by lot from every continent has to refuse on the planetary stage, in public, with reasons — and explain why the voice of humanity, in whose name they keep saying they are developing AI, does not, in fact, matter to them.

As to the unwieldiness, we believe careful facilitation and the judicious deployment of AI tools can make it a nonissue. The 1,000 people could be convened on a virtual platform and the deliberations broken down into small-group discussions followed by different styles of plenary meetings with expert testimonies. Organizers of virtual deliberative polls already know how to run these kinds of meetings efficiently and productively. Meanwhile, AI tools can translate, sort contributions and help members see both where they disagree and where they overlap. Members would keep the authority to judge the summaries, change the agenda and reject the machine’s account of what they meant.

Why choose the participants by lot from every continent rather than rely on a delegation of elected national representatives from every state? Because the stake of any person in the AI race is not conditional on knowledge, credentials or the ability to be elected. Nor is it conditional on the person’s nationality. People who are rarely asked about AI would sit as members of this assembly: the young, the rural, the illiterate, the unconnected, those whose governments would never send them.

To be sure, a lottery does not instantly turn a thousand people into a body legitimately representative of humanity. The assembly would have to earn its moral authority by being exemplary in its procedures and deliberations. Its moral authority would harden into political legitimacy as lawful institutions willingly recognize and take on duties toward it.

The duty to answer, in particular, is the key. Each recommendation from the assembly would go to a named institution, such as a lab or government, with a deadline to respond in public: what it accepts, what it rejects and why. Anyone could challenge a published refusal. Law or enforceable agreement would fix the obligation in advance, as an invitation to advise means nothing when the recipient can ignore it.

One jurisdiction already has enforcement powers of this kind. Since August, the EU’s AI Office can fine a frontier-model provider or order mitigations or a recall. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI have all signed the safety and security chapter of the code of practice that spells out what compliance looks like. Under it, each lab defines its own risk tiers, judges for itself whether its risks are acceptable and picks its own outside evaluators against criteria it publishes.

> “Any lab leader who refuses to answer a thousand people drawn by lot from every continent has to refuse on the planetary stage, in public, with reasons — and explain why the voice of humanity, in whose name they keep saying they are developing AI, does not, in fact, matter to them.”

But in this system, each lab reports to the regulator in full, while the public gets summaries, and only “if and insofar as necessary.” Public consultation comes last among eight ways a lab may gather information, after web searches and market analyses. The most developed safety regime in law to date still treats the public as an input rather than a party. Our proposal would make the global public a party, and the EU could make that enforceable: A clause in a revised code of practice obliging signatories to answer a global assembly’s recommendations in public would give the duty to answer its first legal anchor, in a market no frontier lab can afford to leave.

But what about Beijing? The Chinese Communist Party has repeatedly denounced “exclusive groups” in AI governance, a thinly veiled reference to U.S.-led coalitions, and it has built its own multilateral frameworks, from its Global AI Governance Initiative to a World AI Cooperation Organization launched this summer in Shanghai. A body drawn by lot from every continent is the least Western-dominated forum on offer: By population alone, roughly one seat in six would belong to someone living in China. Beijing may still refuse to let these people take their seats. But the assembly does not need Beijing’s permission to change the game. Washington’s case against restraint rests on the claim that Beijing would never hold its post; a standing body to which people from both sides are invited, and before which each government is asked to answer publicly, turns that claim into a testable one. If Beijing stays away, the world will notice the distance between its rhetoric of inclusive governance and its conduct. If it participates, and, for example, opens its own labs to evaluators vetted under rules the assembly sets, the hunt for the stag has its two most important hunters in the same room.

Key parts of this proposal have been tried. More than 800 deliberative bodies similar to the one we propose have been convened around the world, according to the OECD. There exist several precedents at the global level. In 2021, the Global Assembly for COP26 drew 100 people by a worldwide location lottery to deliberate on climate change before the Glasgow summit. The Metaverse Community Forum on Bullying and Harassment, run by Meta, Stanford’s Deliberative Democracy Lab and the Behavioural Insights Team, convened more than 6,300 people across 32 countries and nine regions of the world in December 2022. In 2023, Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project asked about a thousand Americans to draft principles for an Anthropic model. In March 2024, Taiwan’s Ministry of Digital Affairs, which was led by one of the authors of this essay, worked with the Collective Intelligence Project to text 200,000 random numbers and bring 447 people online to deliberate on AI and information integrity.

How do we get from here to there? We can start with the willing.

First, a small coalition of governments and foundations can fund the assembly through an independent civic secretariat that convenes it on the terms above. That alone would create a focal point no lab or state controls.

Second, Anthropic has committed to letting embedded evaluators publish without its editorial control, and OpenAI has promised to follow. Both could go further: open their labs to evaluators vetted under rules the assembly sets, route what those evaluators find to the assembly, and accept a duty to answer it, on the record and within a fixed deadline, stating what they accept, what they reject and why. Labs that accept this would go a long way toward settling the inner race among themselves and change the outer one: Washington’s restraint would no longer be a unilateral gift to Beijing, but a verified, conditional offer, made before a witness, that Beijing is invited to join.

Third, participating labs can make pacing measurable now. They could pilot a transparent safety-research budget of 5% to 20% of their compute, under published accounting rules, alongside explicit limits on the compute used to accelerate capability research — giving evaluators something concrete to check. A separate allocation could fund public-use computing, with affected communities choosing the projects and judging what they are worth. No public benefit could be traded for a breach of a safety limit.

Is there enough time? If we start today, a first cohort can be seated by spring and deliberating through the rest of 2027. Urgency should not be an excuse to short-circuit public deliberation, and frontier development must stay answerable to it. And if it turns out the end of the world is not as imminent as predicted, and critics are right that the hype merely serves lucrative public offerings, we will still have built a way for humanity to take up, together, the problems that belong to all of it, from AI to climate, terrorism and migration.

Three CEOs have said the frontier must be paced. The racers cannot decide that pace alone; they need a witness they all trust. Let the people be that witness: Give them a seat, a say in the terms and a right to an answer. We should build the assembly now, while we can still set the terms.

title: Why is the human body so crap except for the liver?
content:
[DYNOMIGHT](http://dynomight.net/)

![Image 1](http://dynomight.net/img/liver/killer-whale.jpg)![Image 2](http://dynomight.net/img/liver/killer-whale.jpg)![Image 3](http://dynomight.net/img/liver/killer-whale.jpg)![Image 4](http://dynomight.net/img/liver/killer-whale.jpg)![Image 5](http://dynomight.net/img/liver/killer-whale.jpg)

[_Epistemic Status:_ Speculative unifying theory of biology.]

I don’t know about you, but I greatly resent having to be a biological organism and subject to all the poor engineering and design decisions that entails. This has many manifestations. A recent one is often wondering, why is the entire body such garbage _except for the liver?_

Take the kidneys. Once you reach adulthood, they start to slowly decay. You can damage them through not-obviously-dangerous stuff like taking too much [vitamin D](https://dynomight.net/vitamin-d/) or [taking ibuprofen while dehydrated](https://asteriskmag.com/issues/14/the-mystery-in-the-medicine-cabinet). Significant damage typically leads to scarring and a permanent reduction in function. Or take the gums. If you brush too hard or don’t floss enough, they may retreat down your teeth, never to return. Most of the body is like that.

But the liver. My friends, the liver! If it’s injured, it will usually heal without scars. As you age, it typically maintains near full strength. You can give half of your liver to someone else and it will regrow to full size and function in a few months. I’d like to find whoever designed the liver and have them make me a full body.

Except here’s a theory: It’s good that most of the body is fragile crap. It would be better if some parts of the body were _more_ fragile.

## Some other ways the body would appear to be poorly designed

**Menopause.** We’re still struggling to reconcile modernity with the short human reproductive interval. But did you know that menopause is almost unknown outside of humans? Even the other great apes remain fertile for almost their entire lives. The only known exceptions are (1) killer whales, (2) pilot whales, (3) beluga whales, (4) false killer whales, (5) narwhals, and (6) [one specific population of chimpanzees in Uganda](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.add5473).

**Inuries.** If your leg gets chopped off, that’s it, no more leg. Your body will try to grow scar tissue over the wound and then you’re on your own. But if you chop off the leg of a _salamander_ it… grows a new leg. Isn’t that the obvious thing to do? Why don’t we do that?

**Telomeres.** The ends of your chromosomes have a little repetitive sequence called a telomere. When cells divide, the body tries to copy the DNA, but good-old [DNA polymerase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_polymerase) can’t quite copy all the way to the end, meaning the telomeres slowly get shorter. After dividing [50-70 times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayflick_limit), the telomeres are gone, and the cells stop dividing and then slowly stop working. This is one of the many ticking clocks of aging.

**Transplants.** If you need a new kidney, and someone is nice enough to [give you](https://dynomight.net/money/) one of theirs, your body will respond by trying to kill it, meaning you have to take horrible immunosuppressants for the rest of your life. And even after taking them, there’s a [30%](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.16463) chance the kidney will be rejected within 10 years. This is not helpful.

**Diabetes.** Some day, your immune system may decide to attack your pancreas. After a while, your pancreas will stop making insulin, meaning that unless you reorient your entire life around keeping your blood sugar in check, your eyes, kidneys, nerves, and heart will constantly accumulate damage. Your immune system should not attack your pancreas.

**Brains.** After you reach adulthood, neurons don’t divide. If some of your neurons die—which happens every day—then they’re gone. If you get a brain injury, the other neurons will try to “learn around” the injury, but the neurons themselves are never replaced.

**Junk.** All cells build up various “junk” over time. As they divide, the junk is diluted. But some cells (neurons, various cells in the eyes) never divide, so the amount of junk (e.g. [lipofuscin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lipofuscin#Relation_to_diseases)) just goes up and up. This is another ticking clock.

**Blood.** Your flesh needs blood, which your body delivers through blood vessels. Over time, these can get clogged with plaque. The thing to do in this situation is to sprout new blood vessels. Your body knows how to do that. But by default it maintains high levels of various inhibitors (angiostatin, endostatin, THBS1) that tell your cells not to do so. If your heart or brain get starved of blood, your body will try to reverse all this inhibition, but the process is slow and clumsy and can only produce tiny blood vessels.

## What’s going on here?

As always in biology, the correct answer is: A lot, it’s complicated. But I think there’s a common thread.

The clearest case is probably telomeres wearing down as you get older. At first glance, you might ask, why does this problem exist at all? Bacteria—because they aren’t idiots—have _circular_ DNA, which doesn’t have ends or telomeres. Eukaryotes like us evolved from bacteria. Who decided to replace circular DNA with linear DNA?

Or, you might ask, why doesn’t the body re-lengthen the telomeres? Well, actually it does! We have an enzyme designed specifically for that purpose, called [telomerase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telomerase). But, after embryonic development, the body doesn’t bother to use it, except in stem cells, reproductive cells, and certain parts of the immune system. Huh?

The reason we have linear DNA instead of circular DNA is contested.[1](http://dynomight.net/liver#fn:1)
Some people think linear DNA is easier to copy. Others think that linear DNA just happened by accident, but when it happened it was survivable because we happened to have retrotransposons, i.e. bits of DNA that build little machines to create new copies of their DNA and insert it into the genome. After the break in the circular chromosome, those machines started putting copies of their DNA on the end, because that’s what they do, and this made the break survivable. Those retrotransposons later became telomerase.

 But whatever. If the body wanted to re-lengthen the telomeres, it could easily do that. Your cells already have DNA to make telomerase. They just don’t use it. Instead, they let the telomeres get shorter until they stop dividing and stop working. Why?

Because…

…

Cancer.

(That’s our answer to the question in the title of this post: The human body is so crap except for the liver because cancer. As we’ll see, this answer is only semi-correct, and even then only with several caveats. But what do you expect from biology?)

Letting the telomeres get shorter is not a mistake. It is a deliberate design decision.[2](http://dynomight.net/liver#fn:2)
This is teleological; let’s not let it come between us.

 Often, in your body, the following happens:

1.   Some cells get a mutation that causes them to start reproducing too fast.
2.   Your immune system decides they’re suspicious and kills them.
3.   You’re fine. 👍

But sometimes this happens:

1.   Some cells get a mutation that causes them to start reproducing too fast.
2.   They grow for a while, but then (for complicated reasons[3](http://dynomight.net/liver#fn:3)
This could happen because your immune system contains them. Or because oxygen and nutrients can’t diffuse inside the clump of mutated cells. Or because they run into a barrier of different cell types that they can’t outcompete. Or for other reasons.

) they stop increasing in number.
3.   But they aren’t just sitting there, they’re constantly reproducing and dying, much faster than normal cells.
4.   Eventually, they develop another mutation that allows them to overcome whatever was stopping them from growing.
5.   This continues for a while, with the cells gradually acquiring more of the mutations they need to grow to a large size.
6.   But wait!
7.   With all this reproduction, at some point the mutated cells ran out of telomeres and stopped being able to reproduce.
8.   Ha! Screw you, mutated cells! 👍

To be clear, this also sometimes happen:

1.   (Steps 1-6 above)
2.   With all this reproduction, at some point the mutated cells figured out how to turn telomerase back on.
3.   This re-lengthens their telomeres, so they can reproduce indefinitely.
4.   They either stop growing for other reasons (👍) or you use our modern technological civilization to kill/remove them (👍) or they grow so slowly that something else kills you first (🤌) or there is a less desirable outcome (👎).

(If you’re a biologist who is outraged at the above description, I’ve written a footnote which I beg you read before yelling at me.[4](http://dynomight.net/liver#fn:4)
Hello biologists!

1.   You might be thinking, “_Well actually_, 90% of cancers turn telomerase back on; clearly telomeres don’t help that much; Dynomight why are you so bad?”
2.   That is approximately what the Dynomight Biologist thought, when pressed into service to review this post.
3.   True, having telomeres that wear down is not a magic bullet that makes cancer impossible. And yes, most cancers figure out how to turn telomerase on. But that is a _linguistic_ fact. Your body has lots of mutated cells all over the place, most of which will never hurt you. Conceivably, we could have defined all mutated cells as “cancer”, with subcategories of “low risk to health” and “significant risk to health”. Then, telomeres would seem great, because it’s hard for cells to move from “low risk” to “high risk” without figuring out how to turn telomerase on. That’s hard to do through blind random mutation, which is one reason most of your mutated cells are in the “low risk” category. Cells do sometimes succeed in turning telomerase on, but it’s still a useful layer in body’s layered cancer defense strategy.
4.   We didn’t happen to define our words that way. Instead, we defined “cancer” to mean approximately “mutated cells that pose a significant risk to health” and we’ve invented other categories for other mutated cells (benign neoplasm, clonal expansion, hyperplasia, etc.) The “cancer” category excludes most cells that don’t turn telomerase on _because_ telomere shortening is a good (albeit leaky) barrier between mutated cells and risks to your health. Just because Vikings sometimes get past your city wall doesn’t mean that a city wall is not worth having.
5.   Thank you for visiting my footnote.

)

Having telomeres that wear down is good, because it slows down cancer. It’s also bad, because it means our bodies slowly stop working. Evolution decided the good outweighed the bad, and I expect that evolution was right.

Several of the other ways in which the human body is “crap” can be explained in the same way. Why can’t you re-grow your leg if it gets chopped off? Well, that would require that all your cells have a “begin rapid growth mode” button on them, with some external trigger. In a sense, it would require your body to leave your cells sitting around in a state that’s closer to being cancer. Not doing that is good, because it slows down cancer, and bad, because you can’t grow a new leg. Evolution apparently doesn’t like that tradeoff, and again I assume evolution is right.[5](http://dynomight.net/liver#fn:5)
The precise reasons that salamanders can regrow limbs but most species can’t is somewhat unclear. You could speculate that salamanders tend to lose limbs more frequently, so it’s more worth it for them to pay the “cancer tax”. Or you could speculate that cancer isn’t as much of an issue due to their short lifetime. But _do_ they actually have an unusually high frequency of needing to regrow limbs? And _are_ they paying some kind of cancer tax? What would we even look at to determine that? Cancer rates vary in different animals for all kinds of reasons.

Fragile kidneys are much the same. We _could_ have kidneys that try harder to repair themselves. That’s probably biologically possible. But it would likely mean more kidney cancer. Arguably, the question isn’t, “Why are the kidneys such fragile crap?” but rather, “Why is the liver so weirdly regenerative?”

## OK, so why is the liver so weirdly regenerative?

That question has two standard answers. Answer #1 is that the liver has a hard job. It sits directly downstream of the gut. If you eat toxins or bacterial products or viruses or parasites, the liver sees them at high concentrations before the rest of the body. Not only that, it’s the liver’s job to detoxify stuff, and detoxification chemistry is often [self-damaging](https://asteriskmag.com/issues/14/the-mystery-in-the-medicine-cabinet#:~:text=How%20does%20this%20happen%3F): The liver breaks toxic stuff down into even-more toxic stuff, and then deals with that stuff recursively. The liver is constantly getting damaged, as part of its job description, so it _must_ be able to regenerate. Evolution designed it to do that, and it just pays the cancer tax.

Answer #2 is that the liver _isn’t_ unusual. Your skin can survive wounds. And your intestines can survive exposure to digestive enzymes, bile, and bacteria. The surface layers of both of these are constantly turning over. And, lo and behold, skin cancer and colorectal cancer are both very common.

At the other end of the spectrum, neurons and cardiac muscle cells don’t reproduce after childhood. If they die, they’re gone.[6](http://dynomight.net/liver#fn:6)
Dead cardiac muscle is replaced with scar tissue. Dead neurons are replaced with a “[brain scar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glial_scar)” made of glial cells.

 As a result, “heart cancer” is almost unheard of. (The very term “heart cancer” almost sounds ungrammatical.) Brain cancer is a thing, but it’s essentially always in [other](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glia)[types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meninges) of brain cells, not neurons.

So maybe we can think of different parts of the body as making different tradeoffs between regeneration and cancer risk:[7](http://dynomight.net/liver#fn:7)
Thyroid cancer risk is hard to rate, because it’s common but has a very low fatality rate.

| Organ | Regeneration | Cancer risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Colon / rectum | Extremely high | High |
| Bone marrow | Extremely high | High |
| Skin | High | High |
| Liver | High | High-ish |
| Bladder | High | High-ish |
| Thyroid | Medium | Medium? |
| Kidneys | Low | Low-ish |
| Cardiac muscle | Near zero | Very low |
| Neurons | Near zero | Near zero |

At first glance, we seem to have a cute little story: Evolution pays the cancer tax for organs that need to interface with the environment, because it’s a harsh world out there. And it pays the fragility tax for organs that can be tucked away so that regeneration isn’t as necessary.

Wouldn’t that be nice? Let’s formalize that as a theory.

**Theory:**

*   More regeneration implies more cancer risk.
*   Evolution tunes organs that encounter the environment for more regeneration and more cancer. It tunes organs that don’t for the opposite.

Of course, it’s not that simple.

## Complexities

One problem with the above theory is that it isn’t clear that regeneration is always an option. The skin and guts are pretty homogeneous (at least in each layer). The liver can be approximated as a big blob of repeated [functional units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobules_of_liver). If you give half your liver away, those functional units get larger, which is how your liver grows back to near full size and function.

But other organs are highly “structured”. Your neurons are a complex circuit encoding all your memories and learned behaviors. If neurons were reproducing, that circuit might be unstable.

Your heart is also highly structured. And even if your heart _could_ re-grow, if you lost half of it, you wouldn’t survive long enough to do so. (Do not attempt to donate half your heart.) In principle, it’s surely physically possible to design a heart where you can remove half and it will still pump enough blood to keep you alive while it re-grows. But evolution either didn’t figure that out, or didn’t think it was worth the trouble. Either way, with the current heart design, high regeneration doesn’t look like an option.

So it’s not as simple as evolution choosing to pay the cancer tax for some organs and choosing to pay the fragility tax for others. Some organs need to maintain a stable complex structure to keep working, meaning there may not be much of a cancer/fragility knob to turn.

**Revised theory:**

*   More regeneration implies more cancer risk.
*   Evolution tunes organs that encounter the environment for more regeneration and more cancer. It tunes organs that don’t for the opposite.
*   _But for highly structured organs, regeneration might not be an option._

Fine. But there are several organs I didn’t include in the above table. For example, look at this:

| Organ | Regeneration | Cancer risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lungs | Low-ish | High |

The lungs are the worst of all possible worlds, with low regeneration _and_ high cancer. As far as I can tell, this is a consequence of the physical fact that gas diffusion is slow. To work around that, your lungs have a delicate fractal geometry that crams ~100 square meters of surface area into a ~5 liter volume. That’s impressive, but it makes regeneration hard. At the same time, the lungs need to interface with all sorts of random toxins and pathogens in the air, meaning lots of ways for mutations to happen.

**Revised theory v2:**

*   More regeneration implies more cancer risk.
*   Evolution tunes organs that encounter the environment for more regeneration and more cancer. It tunes organs that don’t for the opposite.
*   But for highly structured organs, regeneration might not be an option.
*   _And if highly structured organs encounter the environment, cancer risk is still high._

And now, ladies and gentlemen, the stupid pancreas:

| Organ | Regeneration | Cancer risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pancreas | Low-ish | Moderate |

Superficially, this looks less exceptional than the lungs, with low-ish regeneration and merely moderate cancer risk. But the pancreas is more problematic for our theory, because that moderate cancer risk exists despite not being exposed to the outside world.

Biologically, the reasons that the pancreas sometimes develops cancer seem [understood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KRAS), although complex. But as far as I can tell, there is no convincing explanation for why the pancreas is designed that way. Is it an evolutionary fluke? Is there some other subtle tradeoff? It’s unclear. So there’s no satisfying big-picture evolutionary trade-off to point to.

**Revised theory v3:**

*   More regeneration implies more cancer risk.
*   Evolution tunes organs that encounter the environment for more regeneration and more cancer. It tunes organs that don’t for the opposite.
*   But for highly structured organs, regeneration might not be an option.
*   And if highly structured organs encounter the environment, cancer risk is still high.
*   _And the pancreas is weird._

But we still need to face the final boss, the strangest organ of all.

## The small intestine

| Organ | Regeneration | Cancer risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small intestine | Extremely high | Very low |

Bad news for our theory, good news for you as a biological organism. The small intestine _does_ interface with the environment, and it replaces all its surface-level cells every few days. Yet it very rarely develops cancer. That’s despite the fact that it’s quite similar to the cancer-crazed colon. It’s _also_ despite the fact that the “small” intestine makes up ~90% of the digestive tract’s surface area. What the hell?

Biologically, the main explanation seems to be that the small intestine uses an ingenious defense strategy. My new favorite part of the body:

![Image 6](http://dynomight.net/img/liver/Gray1059.png)

While the surface cells of the small intestine are continuously being replaced, they aren’t themselves reproducing. Instead, [carefully protected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paneth_cell) stem cells tucked into the valleys between the [intestinal villi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intestinal_villus) slowly produce “transit-amplifying cells”. Those transit-amplifying cells divide 4-6 times as they migrate to the surface, each eventually yielding 16-64 mature epithelial cells. Those spend a few days doing epithelial stuff, meanwhile sliding along with their siblings from the bottom to the top of whichever villus they happen to be on. When they reach the tip, they’re ejected into the digestive stream to die, merry Christmas. So, even if a mutation arises somewhere, it doesn’t really matter, because the cells are all on a conveyor belt towards death anyway.

Clever, no? Turns out, the real hero isn’t the liver. It’s the small intestine.

(The small intestine also uses a few other tricks: The surface cells are programmed to commit suicide if damaged even a little bit. The immune system is tuned to kill anything that looks even slightly funny. And it hosts huge amounts of detoxifying enzymes. But villi seem to be the really unique bit.)

This is a huge challenge for our theory. Not only does the small intestine have low cancer and high regeneration, it has low cancer _because_ of high regeneration. If the small intestine can do that, then why not the rest of the body?

One answer is that it takes a ton of energy. Your guts shed ~40 billion epithelial cells every day, amounting to ~⅓ kg of tissue every week. Like the brain, your guts consume ~20% of total energy, despite making up only ~2% of body mass. Evolution doesn’t want to do that everywhere, because evolution doesn’t want you to starve to death.

So, there isn’t just a trade-off between regeneration and cancer. There’s a three-way tradeoff between regeneration, cancer, and energy usage.

![Image 7](http://dynomight.net/img/liver/triangle.svg)

But even if energy weren’t an issue, other organs couldn’t easily copy the small intestine’s strategy. For example, the colon is similar in many ways to the small intestine, but the colon doesn’t have villi. It needs to be flat, because the colon’s job is to extract water. If there were villi dangling everywhere, they’d be ripped off by the solid waste. The colon also hosts far more bacteria that produce toxic byproducts, meaning the colon’s cells need to be tuned to try to resist damage, instead of committing suicide. This also means that the immune system needs to be more relaxed about killing foreign entities. So even though the colon _also_ replaces the epithelial cells (a bit more slowly) cancer is still common.

(Or, imagine your skin was covered in tiny fragile villi. You’d look awesome, but they’d be constantly getting ripped off. If you wanted that to work, you’d need to make the villi stronger and more disposable, and… we just invented fur.)

**Revised theory v4 final (actually final) updated (2):**

*   More regeneration implies more cancer risk.
*   Evolution tunes organs that encounter the environment for more regeneration and more cancer. It tunes organs that don’t for the opposite.
*   But for highly structured organs, regeneration might not be an option.
*   And if highly structured organs encounter the environment, cancer risk is still high.
*   And the pancreas is weird.
*   _And actually, it’s not just a trade-off between regeneration and cancer, it’s a three-way trade-off between regeneration and cancer and energy usage, and various parts of that space may or may not be available depending on the job an organ has to do_.

So, a cancer vs. fragility tradeoff definitely doesn’t explain everything. But it does explain some things, somewhat, sort of. In biology, that’s pretty good.

## Is this bad?

We’ve discussed various ways in which the body might appear to be crap. Let’s revisit those, and ask if the right tradeoff is being made for the modern world.

**Injuries.**

Your skin is calibrated for constant wounds, which most of us today don’t get. This leaves lots of repair pathways sitting around to be hijacked by skin cancer. Similarly, your bone marrow is calibrated to be able to recover from catastrophic blood loss. Today we don’t experience as much catastrophic blood loss, and we have blood transfusions, but all that generative capacity is still there to be used by leukemia and lymphoma. And whatever benefit there might have been to re-growing a limb is probably lower today, when we less often lose limbs.

Best guess: It would be better if the body tried _less_ hard to recover from injuries.

**Brains.**

Do modern people suffer fewer brain injuries than our evolutionary ancestors? It’s hard to say for sure, because brains are soft tissue. But the fossil record for upper paleolithic humans suggests [between 2% and 34%](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0696-8) suffered skull fractures, more than modern people.

So you might think it would be better if the brain was tuned more towards fragility rather than cancer. But brain injuries are still common today. Around ⅓ of people experience a concussion sometime in their lifetime, because we love to drive cars at high speed, play dangerous sports, and survive to old age where stairs and bathrooms pose a risk. Also, for whatever reason, the brain is _already_ tuned quite strongly towards fragility.

Best guess: Maybe the current tradeoff is about right?

**Telomeres.**

Should the body re-lengthen the telomeres? On the one hand, we’re more likely to survive to ages where this is actually an issue. On the other hand, we’re also more likely to survive to ages where cancer is a danger, which is precisely where telomeres _not_ getting re-lengthened is an issue.

Best guess: Maybe the current tradeoff is about right?

**Livers.**

It seems that the liver is so regenerative because it _needed_ to be. Ancestral humans were constantly dealing with parasites and bacteria and rotting food. When I started writing this essay, I figured this meant the liver was “over-specced” for the modern world. Today we have refrigerators and food inspectors and pasteurization. Our lives are much less harsh and involve fewer toxins than our ancestors. So, if calibrated for the modern environment, I figured that it would be better if the liver was a bit more fragile, but also marginally less prone to cancer.[8](http://dynomight.net/liver#fn:8)
You wouldn’t want to make the liver unable to regenerate, but there are several “knobs” that might be tuned. Broadly speaking, the liver could be designed to regenerate more slowly, with more careful “proofreading” and slower/stricter cell-cycle checkpointing. Then liver injuries would take longer to heal, but would result in fewer mutated cells.

But… it’s not clear that this is actually true. Liver failure remains extremely common today. While we don’t ingest nearly as many toxins, we eat diets that lead to metabolic dysfunction, and we consume tons of alcohol, and many of us live in dense conditions where hepatitis can easily spread. We’re also more likely to live to an age where liver failure is an issue.

Best guess: Unclear. We should stop doing stuff that causes liver failure.

**Menopause.**

Why do humans have menopause, unlike almost all other mammals? The most common theory is the [grandmother hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmother_hypothesis). The general idea is that reproducing becomes more and more risky as you get older. For most animals, evolution doesn’t care, because evolution’s goal isn’t to make you happy, it’s to maximize reproductive fitness. So, screw it, try to reproduce and let the dice fall where they may. But even after reproducing, _humans_ can help the survival of their genes by providing resources for their offspring. So, for humans, evolution decided to turn reproduction off, so you can spend more time with your grandkids.

In particular, with cancer, some theorize that continued cycles of estrogen cause damage to the ovaries, womb, and breasts. Menopause shuts this down,which may decrease the odds of ovarian / uterine / breast cancer.

It’s a cute theory. But again:

*   Menopause: Humans, killer whales, pilot whales, beluga whales, false killer whales, narwhals, one group of chimps in Uganda.
*   No menopause: Everything else, including elephants, other whales, lions, horses, zebras, dogs, rats, wolves, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish.

Some of this makes sense. Unlike toothed whales, Blue/Humpback whales are mostly solitary or live in loose groups. Mice don’t babysit for their grandkids. But what about elephants? Or hyenas? Or bonobos? Or orangutans? Or lions? Or sperm whales? All of these have social organizations where females contribute to the survival of their offspring, and yet they don’t have menopause.

Anyway, is menopause the right tradeoff for the modern age? It’s hard to say. On the one hand, modern people live much longer, meaning the marginal cost of cancer is higher. On the other hand, people want to reproduce more at older ages, meaning menopause has a higher cost. (Both “to evolution” and “to us”.) Also, an ancestral woman began menstruating in her late teens, and then likely underwent many pregnancies, each followed by years-long periods of breastfeeding (which suppresses menstruation). An average modern woman experiences 3-5 times as many menstrual cycles. It’s very confusing.

Best guess: No idea.

**Cell junk / diabetes / transplants.**

As far as I can tell, these are mostly unrelated.

## TLDR

Cancer is bad because cancer is bad. Cancer is _also_ bad because evolution made gruesome _realpolitik_ compromises in the design of every part of the body to try to hold cancer in check. If we lived in a universe where cancer was impossible, we wouldn’t just not get cancer, our bodies would also be enormously more regenerative and longer lasting.

In a sense, even if you don’t get cancer, cancer still hurts you, because your body was forced to take costly preventative actions. (Even if the barbarians never get over your city wall, you still had to build the wall.) Even if we someday completely defeat cancer, its legacy will live on in our genes until the point that we re-design ourselves. Screw cancer.

1.   Some people think linear DNA is easier to copy. Others think that linear DNA just happened by accident, but when it happened it was survivable because we happened to have retrotransposons, i.e. bits of DNA that build little machines to create new copies of their DNA and insert it into the genome. After the break in the circular chromosome, those machines started putting copies of their DNA on the end, because that’s what they do, and this made the break survivable. Those retrotransposons later became telomerase.[↩](http://dynomight.net/liver#fnref:1)

2.   This is teleological; let’s not let it come between us.[↩](http://dynomight.net/liver#fnref:2)

3.   This could happen because your immune system contains them. Or because oxygen and nutrients can’t diffuse inside the clump of mutated cells. Or because they run into a barrier of different cell types that they can’t outcompete. Or for other reasons.[↩](http://dynomight.net/liver#fnref:3)

4.   Hello biologists!

    2.   That is approximately what the Dynomight Biologist thought, when pressed into service to review this post.
    3.   True, having telomeres that wear down is not a magic bullet that makes cancer impossible. And yes, most cancers figure out how to turn telomerase on. But that is a _linguistic_ fact. Your body has lots of mutated cells all over the place, most of which will never hurt you. Conceivably, we could have defined all mutated cells as “cancer”, with subcategories of “low risk to health” and “significant risk to health”. Then, telomeres would seem great, because it’s hard for cells to move from “low risk” to “high risk” without figuring out how to turn telomerase on. That’s hard to do through blind random mutation, which is one reason most of your mutated cells are in the “low risk” category. Cells do sometimes succeed in turning telomerase on, but it’s still a useful layer in body’s layered cancer defense strategy.
    4.   We didn’t happen to define our words that way. Instead, we defined “cancer” to mean approximately “mutated cells that pose a significant risk to health” and we’ve invented other categories for other mutated cells (benign neoplasm, clonal expansion, hyperplasia, etc.) The “cancer” category excludes most cells that don’t turn telomerase on _because_ telomere shortening is a good (albeit leaky) barrier between mutated cells and risks to your health. Just because Vikings sometimes get past your city wall doesn’t mean that a city wall is not worth having.

Or you could speculate that cancer isn’t as much of an issue due to their short lifetime. But _do_ they actually have an unusually high frequency of needing to regrow limbs? And _are_ they paying some kind of cancer tax? What would we even look at to determine that? Cancer rates vary in different animals for all kinds of reasons.[↩](http://dynomight.net/liver#fnref:5)
